title: Chapter 131 — Difficult Conversations
intro: Sometimes you have to deliver news the customer does not want to hear.

sections.title: Delivering Bad News
sections.content:
Backordered six weeks. Discontinued. Price went up. Part not available. Delivery delayed.

Lead with empathy, follow with facts, close with options. 'I know this is not what you want to hear — the model you ordered is backordered for approximately six weeks. Here is what I can do: I can hold your order at today's price and update you weekly on status, or I can show you a comparable model that is in stock right now. What would you prefer?'

Never hide behind email for bad news. Call. The customer deserves to hear your voice and know you care.

sections.title: Managing Unrealistic Expectations
sections.content:
The customer who wants a $3,000 fridge for $1,800. The one who wants delivery tomorrow for an item on backorder. The one who wants free installation because 'it should be included.'

Be honest without being dismissive. 'I understand the budget concern. At $1,800, here is the best option I can offer — it is an excellent product and I think you will be happy with it. The $3,000 model has additional features, but this one covers everything you told me you need.'

sections.title: The Policy Exception
sections.content:
Sometimes bending a rule is the right business decision. Sometimes it is not. The judgment call is: what is the lifetime value of this customer versus the cost of the exception?

A $50 restocking fee on a return for a customer who buys $5,000 per year? Waive it. A full refund on a 6-month-old product with no receipt? That requires a conversation.

Know your authority. Know when to escalate. And when you do bend a rule, frame it as exceptional: 'I do not normally do this, but I want to make this right for you.'
